processing: As with other Yunnan raw pu-erh, the leaf is typically wilted, wok-fired, rolled and sun-dried into mao cha, then sold loose or steamed and pressed; no ripe-style pile fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as is usual for Mengku raw pu-erh; little is documented about the season here beyond that.
appearance_dry: Typical of Mengku large-leaf raw tea: long, thick dark strands with some tip.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear golden yellow when young.
appearance_wet: Thick large leaves in olive green, as with other Mengku raw teas.
taste_profile: Little is documented about Dongguo's own taste. Its old trees are locally rated alongside Bingdao, and Mengku raw tea generally is sweet, fragrant and vigorous.

brewing.notes: General Mengku raw settings, since nothing specific to Dongguo is recorded.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year like other sheng: mostly as spring tea of a stated year, either as loose mao cha or pressed cakes. Young cakes of one to three years are the usual purchase, and those who store it age it for a decade or more. Ask for the year and the tree age, since old-tree and plantation leaf are priced far apart.
description:
Dongguo is the largest village on Mengku's western half-mountain, the seat of a village committee with four natural villages and the biggest tea area on that side of the mountain. It is one of the Mengku Eighteen Villages.

Tea of very different ages grows here: trees of more than 150 years planted by the Lahu, gardens of 60 to 100 years, and newer planting. That range affects the cup more than any special method does, as processing is the usual raw pu-erh one.

No detailed tasting record stands out. Locally the big old trees are said to be no worse than Bingdao's, which is a claim worth testing with a sample, not trusting. Brew as you would a strong young sheng.

Because the area is large, Dongguo on a label covers a wide range of quality. Ask about tree age and which garden, and expect old-tree leaf to cost much more.
history:
The village was Lahu before the reform that replaced native chieftains with appointed officials, and those early households planted its oldest surviving trees.

Gardens planted between 1904 and 1940 are a large part of the present area. The village also housed the primary processing station that took in leaf from neighbouring Baka for a long time.
